posts.author: dave battin
posts.content_md:
infocus #620 projector

I am currently trying to use the afore mentioned projector to try and digitize my holographic images, so i thought i would start a thread to help myself and others that are to make this semi jump into digitized holography. I purchased this unit a few years ago thru ebay and since it had some issues i decided to disassemble the unit to help to understand its workings. I now have purchase two more working units an plan on adapting one for my holo-table. Very little information is available about the workings of these units, so any information is worth its weight in gold. To my surprise while doing searches for this unit i found this link from MIT lab

[http://www.media.mit.edu/spi/SPIPapers/ryder/SPIE99.pdf](http://www.media.mit.edu/spi/SPIPapers/ryder/SPIE99.pdf)

posts.author: favalora
posts.content_md:
Hi Dave - 

That is a good paper. I recall reading it around 2000-01 when my startup was engaged in reverse-engineering the DMD control electronics for our volumetric 3-D display. (It was prior to the DMD being a "catalog part.") We needed to pump 6,000 XGA-resolution frames each second out of them, at 100% duty cycle if needed.

Nowadays, several companies sell DMD controller boards, like Vialux in Germany, with their "ALP" boards. There is also a domestic group whose name I forgot.

I started writing this note and then forgot your question. What's up?

Oh - we don't make displays anymore but we are featured in this week's Economist here: [http://www.economist.com/sciencetechnol ... d=14299526](http://www.economist.com/sciencetechnology/tq/displaystory.cfm?story_id=14299526) -- the 3-D display at top uses 3 DMDs at 6,000 frames/sec at XGA resolution each, for a total of a 100 million voxel display.

g

posts.author: dave battin
posts.content_md:
Wow, that would put this a little out of my holo-budget. seeing how these #620 units cost me @ $100 each i will continue to design my system around them. I think the reason this projector was the choice of the MIT lab is the B+W setting actually pulls the color wheel up and out of the way of the optical path, bypassing the color feedback circuit allowing the unit to operate in "freewheeling mode"

allowing a monochrome (laser light) image to be projected.

thanks for the input guys .............

posts.author: favalora
posts.content_md:
Mike -

Thanks for sharing your paper. I was unable to read it completely at this late hour, so I apologize if I am missing some key details. I wanted to comment that the "capture" might be simpler than you are suggesting. For instance, you can associate a fly's-eye lens array with a high resolution digital camera. That does a fairly good job of capturing a light field, even if very few pixels are behind each lenslet. Are you already familiar with the body of work at Stanford and MIT on light field rendering? (E.g. Ren Ng's fourier slice photography?) Or the (mostly Asian) work in integral photography?

I did not understand your replay geometry, but that is my fault, not yours.

-g
